finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; these are first figures. Shops usually sell a brake fluid flush at a set menu price, not as parts plus clocked labor, so the built totals here are a floor-to-middle view, and a menu price can sit above them. Built totals (fluid + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $71-$189; midsize 2016 Accord about $71-$182; truck 2016 F-150 about $78-$200; luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $76-$179. The classes barely differ because the fluid is cheap ($11-$40 for about a quart) and the labor is the same half hour to an hour. Against the benchmarks: the built range covers Jerry ($80-$130) and CarGurus ($70-$120) and reaches Kelley Blue Book's low end ($173-$205), but it sits below the top of Kelley Blue Book, YourMechanic's shop and dealer figures ($212-$251 for one vehicle) and the $150-$250 a named technician quotes. That gap is what a menu price looks like: shops commonly charge about an hour or more of labor at their own rate regardless of the clock, and dealers charge more per hour. A fair plain-language range is roughly $80-$250, with the built totals explaining the lower two thirds. How solid the numbers are: the labor times that set the range are still general statements (30 minutes to 1 hour; .75 to 1.0 hour from a named technician), not vehicle-specific and not flat-rate book times. A second look on 2026-11-20 changed no number but found one maker time that sits inside the range: Hyundai's warranty table for a 2009-2012 Genesis sedan and 2011-2012 Equus campaign gives 'Brake Fluid Replacement' 0.7 M/H, for a four-wheel fluid replacement plus ten scan-tool flushing cycles of the ABS unit. It is listed under the luxury class as a cross-check only, because it is not the example vehicle, it is a warranty time, and it includes a scan-tool step a routine flush may skip. Two larger maker jobs bracket it and were not used: Hyundai's 1.0 M/H for the same fluid replacement plus an ABS-unit inspection, and Nissan's 2.2 hr campaign flush on the Murano and Quest, which is tied to an ABS actuator concern. Taken together, the maker figures support the half hour to an hour used here and suggest a car that needs a scan-tool ABS cycle lands in the upper half. No Toyota, Honda, Ford or BMW stated time for this service was found; Honda, Acura, GM and Subaru brake bulletins that were loaded print times only for jobs that bundle a part replacement, and GM's bleed operation says to use its published time without printing it. The quantity (about one quart or liter) comes from the Nissan bulletin, not from each maker, and may be on the low side: Hyundai's campaign uses about 1.8 L (five 12 fl oz bottles) and a Mitsubishi recall flush (2006-2009 Eclipse, bulletin SR-15-004REV) uses about 1.3 L, both including an ABS-unit flush; one seller recommends 3-4 pint bottles for a full flush, which would add $20-$40 on the truck. At two liters the fluid would roughly double, adding about $11-$40 depending on the class. The high parts figures for the truck and the BMW are retailer prices for the maker's fluid, because no list price was loaded; the Toyota and Honda figures are list prices. No chain-shop menu price could be loaded: Jiffy Lube's page asks for vehicle details before showing a price, and its cost article gives no dollar figure. RepairPal's page for this job was not found in search.
extras: A quote often adds shop supplies or a fluid disposal fee and sales tax. Vehicles that need a scan tool to cycle the ABS unit during bleeding, and some hybrids, can be billed more time. Seized or broken bleeder screws, leaking calipers or wheel cylinders and cracked brake hoses found during the job are quoted separately. Many shops offer the flush alongside a brake pad job, sometimes at a lower combined price. Performance or low-viscosity fluid costs more than standard DOT 3.
